title: The Sheep, the Wolf, and the Stag
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: A Stag once asked a Sheep to lend him a measure of wheat, saying that his friend the Wolf would be his surety. The Sheep, however, was afraid that they meant to cheat her; so she excused herself, saying, "The Wolf is in the habit of seizing what he wants and running off with it without paying, and you, too, can run much faster than I. So how shall I be able to come up with either of you when the debt falls due?" Two blacks do not make a white.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did the Stag ask the Sheep to lend him?
options: A measure of wheat
A sack of hay
A bag of gold coins
A length of rope

questions.prompt: According to the passage, who did the Stag say would be his surety?
options: His friend the Wolf
His mother
The farmer who owned the field
No one; he offered none

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what was the Sheep afraid of?
options: That they meant to cheat her
That the wheat would spoil
That the Stag would eat her instead
That the Wolf would tell others of the loan

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what habit does the Sheep say the Wolf has?
options: Seizing what he wants and running off without paying
Warning others before he takes anything
Sharing everything he finds with his friends
Repaying debts before they are even due

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Sheep say about the Stag's speed?
options: That he can run much faster than she can
That he is slower than she is
That his speed does not matter to her
That he only runs quickly when frightened

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Sheep ask about the debt falling due?
options: How she would be able to catch up with either of them
Whether the Wolf would remind the Stag of it
Who would decide the exact date it was due
Whether wheat could be repaid with meat instead

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the Sheep decide not to lend the wheat?
options: She realizes that neither the borrower nor the guarantor could actually be held to account if they failed to pay
She simply does not have any wheat to spare
She believes wheat is too valuable to lend to anyone
She is waiting for a better offer from another animal

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the point of the fable, as suggested by its closing line?
options: A promise backed by someone just as untrustworthy as the borrower is no promise at all
Sheep are wiser than every other animal in the forest
Stags and wolves should never be allowed to make agreements
Wheat should only be lent to animals who can run quickly

questions.prompt: According to the passage, who first approached whom to ask for the loan?
options: The Stag approached the Sheep
The Sheep approached the Stag
The Wolf approached the Sheep
The Sheep approached the Wolf

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how does the Sheep describe the way the Wolf takes things?
options: Without paying for them
Only after asking politely first
By trading fairly with others
Only when he is truly desperate

questions.prompt: According to the closing line of the fable, what do two blacks not make?
options: A white
A whole
A right
A debt

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the Sheep mention the Stag's speed alongside the Wolf's habit of seizing things?
options: Both traits would let either animal escape her if she needed to demand repayment
She wants to compliment both animals before refusing them
She is trying to challenge the Stag to a race
She thinks speed and thievery are unrelated to the loan

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "surety" mean in "his friend the Wolf would be his surety"?
options: Someone who guarantees a debt will be paid
Someone who witnesses a crime
A type of measuring container for wheat
A close relative by blood

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: The Sheep lends the wheat once the Wolf promises to repay it himself
The Stag asks the Sheep for a loan backed by the Wolf, but the Sheep refuses since neither animal could be trusted to repay
The Wolf demands wheat from the Sheep and the Stag defends her
The Sheep and the Stag agree to split the wheat between them
